title: The substituted persona's words fit neither Paul nor the baptized; 'sin' names the devil
english: The words spoken in character fit neither the inspired Paul nor anyone buried together with Christ through baptism. Such people have been freed from what is called the flesh. They will no longer be condemned because of Adam's disobedience. Sin no longer reigns over them, nor does the death that comes through sin. They were buried together with the life of Christ, who obliterated disobedience by His obedience and drove out the death that came upon us from it by His voluntary death. For He willingly came under the law of disobedience, so that He might redeem us who were under the law of condemnation. For this reason every redeemed person says: "Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord" (Romans 7:25). For what the law could not do, weakened as it was through the flesh, God did by sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh; He condemned sin in the flesh (Romans 8:3).

That these things have been rightly observed, the divine apostle confirms when he says: "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death" (Romans 8:1-2), and what follows.

Let me now attempt to speak briefly, in passing, about the very words spoken in character, beginning from: "Sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me" (Romans 7:11). The name "sin" does not indicate an existing substance, but rather a manner and way of life of someone who has missed the mark of what is reasonable and correct. For "sin" is a most general name, predicated of many different things. Every sin comes about neither by reason nor by a commanding law. For if it came about according to law and right reason, it would no longer be a sin, since it would have a defined and ordered principle of its origin.

But since the divine apostle mentions not simply sins, but a most general sin that has a mind, that has a law, that is able to devise clever schemes and procure opportunities for the construction of evil, he names no other as sin in the most general sense than the very originator and father of sins, the devil. For this reason the apostle also declared that he reigns over sins: "Let not sin reign in your mortal body" (Romans 6:12). For just as we call people by the craft they practice, so also he calls the devil himself "sin," since he was the first inventor of sin.

So then, through the commandment given to Adam the devil deceived the man, and through it he deceived Adam, procuring opportunities through the commandment. The devil says: "Why is it that God said, 'You shall not eat from every tree in the garden'? But on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil." He cleverly devises to conceal the deception with a greater promise. He promises more, so that he might overturn the guardians of the commandment from the foundations of virtue by a fall like his own. For having goaded the man to want to become equal to God, he procured the opportunity for the deceptive conversation from the commandment that had been given. For this reason Paul said: "Sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me" (Romans 7:11).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Didymus is explaining why the words of Romans 7, spoken in a substituted persona, cannot apply to Paul or to any Christian buried with Christ in baptism, and he begins to identify 'sin' as the devil.

title: The commandment is holy; sin became sinful beyond measure
english: But so that no one might blame the commandment or the God who gave it, he used a closely related and kindred word, saying: "We know that the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good" (Romans 7:12). Since not even sin itself—that is, the devil—is sin by nature and substance, he adds: "so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment" (Romans 7:13). For what is something by substance will not admit degrees of more and less; it is what it is, always being what it is essentially. But for what comes to be and has something added to it, whether little or beyond measure, it is other in substance than the things added to it. Quantity is not substance but is an attribute of substance, not being substance. Therefore the one called sin by the apostle admits the more of sinning, so that sin might become sinful beyond measure. So sin also received a beginning of being sin, insofar as it is sin, not being sinful beyond measure in the beginning according to its having sinned. Therefore he also signifies the intensification of becoming sinful beyond measure in time to come, saying: "so that sin might become sinful beyond measure through the commandment" (Romans 7:13). But if objectors should say: How could the commandment and the law be good and just? How could they be holy, when through the opportunity they provided sin became sinful beyond measure? Let those who object hear in response that if something is harmed, the opportunity through which it is harmed is not therefore already base and evil. For it is not because those who gaze at the sun without method and without measure harm their eyes that we therefore call the sun evil. Nor is it because the devil became sinful beyond measure by having attacked the Son of God that we therefore say the Son of God is base and evil. "I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh" (Romans 7:18). Now Paul explains this as spoken in the person of Adam. And because he was deprived of having God in himself, he took death in exchange for true life—for not only the common death of his members took hold of him, but also the death of disobedience entered against his soul. For the ruling death reigned especially before the coming of Christ, having disobedience as the law and scepter of its kingdom over all. But the kingdom of death is not without beginning or unbegotten; for dying comes about from the living, and someone's disobedience comes about from the obedience of those who obey. "For the will is present with me, but the working out of the good is not. For the good I will, this I do not do; but what I hate, this I practice" (Romans 7:18-19). If only the willing is in us, and the accomplishment of the willed good is not in us, then the good God sent souls of the same substance as himself into bodies in vain. For they do not do what is dear to him and to them; they do not enact it, but only will it—and perhaps not even that, for even the willing is unclear.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Didymus is explaining Paul's words in Romans 7, arguing that the commandment and law are holy, just, and good, and that 'sin' means the devil, who became sinful beyond measure through the commandment.

title: The devil, not the flesh, works sin in us
english: But if this is true, I will reason as the impious do: then the good never was and never will be in life, nor did anyone ever accomplish it, if they take the words "the good I will, this I do not do; but what I hate, this I practice" (Romans 7:19) as the abolition of the good and beautiful for every human being. And from where did the names of virtues ever appear in human life? But if there are those who do the good, even if only a few do it, then not everyone will say, "We know that good does not dwell in us"; for the good they willed, this they do. If those who enact the good do so while existing in flesh, and those who do not do this but do evil are also in flesh, then the cause of the good not coming about must not be attached to the flesh, but to the weakness of these people's souls. For if evil dwells beside those who will to do the good, Keep the English unchanged: "and likewise the good lies beside those who will to do evil,". Add to translator_notes: "u01-rem-close: the locked text reads οὐ καλὸν παράκειται; we translate as τὸ καλὸν παράκειται, because ὁμοίως and the parallel with Rom 7:21 (ἐμοὶ τὸ κακὸν παράκειται) call for it. Taken literally, the transmitted text would say 'what is not good lies beside those who will to do evil.'" and after foreseeing and willing beforehand they come to such a degree of action, then our bodies are not evil by nature or substance. For deliberation and willing lead the way before our actions, and these belong to a soul that has free will, able to incline toward whatever actions it chooses.

"But now it is no longer I who do it, but the sin dwelling in me" (Romans 7:17). Through this saying he has defended the point that the flesh is not evil by nature. For it is not the flesh we are clothed in that dwells in us, but the devil who dwells in the lawless. For just as I say that Christ dwells in every righteous person who works the good, in the same way I think the devil dwells in every evildoer. Therefore we are not evil insofar as we have flesh, but the sin dwelling in us is, and it is something other than the flesh and the soul of the human being. For the devil is said to dwell especially in the soul, according to "Satan entered into the heart of Judas" (cf. John 13:2, 27), and according to "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart?" (Acts 5:3).

It was well said too: "no longer I work it out, but the sin dwelling in me." For there is a great distance between a work and a working-out, because the preparation precedes the finished work, as, for example, of a house or a ship. The working-out is the prior preparation of the material. So the sin dwelling in those who sin, that is, Satan, admittedly works out beforehand in our reasonings the form of the evil to come, the construction, while the soul that has received him cooperates with him in the evil, just as the womb of the female cooperates with those who sow, so that what is sown may be brought to completion. And since evil reasonings come forth from the heart, from the conception of the devil that has taken place, the divine saying cries out: "we destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God" (2 Corinthians 10:5). Just as the Holy Spirit is said to labor together with virtue-loving souls, according to "I labored more abundantly than all of them, yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me" (1 Corinthians 15:10), so when a careless soul is persuaded by the devil's urgings, it has the devil himself as a coworker toward evil. For he himself has worked out beforehand in it the pattern of the sin to come. For this reason it is said: "no longer I work it out, but the sin dwelling in me" (Romans 7:17).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Didymus is answering an impious objection to Paul's words in Romans 7:18-19, arguing that if no one can do the good they will, then virtue would be impossible, and he now explains that the indwelling sin is the devil, not the flesh.
